AI.motivation: To understand the underlying mechanism of instruction-following in language models - whether it relies on a universal mechanism or compositional skill deployment, given that instruction tuning is commonly assumed to endow models with domain-general ability to follow instructions but the mechanism remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Diagnostic probing across nine diverse tasks in three instruction-tuned models using: 1) General vs. task-specific probes to test representational sharing, 2) Cross-task transfer analysis to examine skill similarity clustering, 3) Causal ablation to identify dependencies, 4) Layer-wise analysis of task stratification by complexity, and 5) Temporal analysis of constraint satisfaction during generation.
AI.result: 1) General probes consistently underperform task-specific specialists, indicating limited representational sharing. 2) Cross-task transfer is weak and clustered by skill similarity. 3) Causal ablation reveals sparse asymmetric dependencies rather than shared representations. 4) Tasks stratify by complexity across layers (structural constraints emerge early, semantic tasks emerge late). 5) Constraint satisfaction operates as dynamic monitoring during generation rather than pre-generation planning.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-following is better characterized as skillful coordination of diverse linguistic capabilities rather than deployment of a single abstract constraint-checking process, with evidence against a universal mechanism.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Structure of Mathematics
summary: Recent progress in artificial intelligence (AI) is unlocking transformative capabilities for mathematics. There is great hope that AI will help solve major open problems and autonomously discover new mathematical concepts. In this essay, we further consider how AI may open a grand perspective on mathematics by forging a new route, complementary to mathematical\textbf{ logic,} to understanding the global structure of formal \textbf{proof}\textbf{s}. We begin by providing a sketch of the formal structure of mathematics in terms of universal proof and structural hypergraphs and discuss questions this raises about the foundational structure of mathematics. We then outline the main ingredients and provide a set of criteria to be satisfied for AI models capable of automated mathematical discovery. As we send AI agents to traverse Platonic mathematical worlds, we expect they will teach us about the nature of mathematics: both as a whole, and the small ribbons conducive to human understanding. Perhaps they will shed light on the old question: "Is mathematics discovered or invented?" Can we grok the terrain of these \textbf{Platonic worlds}?

AI.tldr: AI can transform mathematics by analyzing formal proof structures through universal proof hypergraphs, potentially revealing mathematics' foundational nature and addressing whether math is discovered or invented.
AI.motivation: Recent AI progress offers potential to solve major open mathematical problems and autonomously discover new concepts. The paper aims to explore how AI can provide a new perspective on understanding the global structure of formal proofs, complementary to mathematical logic, and potentially answer fundamental questions about the nature of mathematics.
AI.method: Proposes analyzing mathematics through universal proof and structural hypergraphs as a formal framework. Outlines criteria for AI models capable of automated mathematical discovery, enabling AI agents to explore "Platonic mathematical worlds" and analyze proof structures.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework for using AI to understand mathematical proof structures, but does not provide empirical results. It establishes theoretical foundations for how AI could reveal the global organization of mathematics and potentially answer philosophical questions about mathematics' nature.
AI.conclusion: AI has the potential to transform our understanding of mathematics by providing new perspectives on proof structures and foundational questions. By sending AI agents to explore mathematical spaces, we may gain insights into whether mathematics is discovered or invented and understand the "terrain" of Platonic mathematical worlds.

title: Claw-Eval: Toward Trustworthy Evaluation of Autonomous Agents
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents executing multi-step workflows in real-world software environments. However, existing agent benchmarks suffer from three critical limitations: (1) trajectory-opaque grading that checks only final outputs, (2) underspecified safety and robustness evaluation, and (3) narrow modality coverage and interaction paradigms. We introduce Claw-Eval, an end-to-end evaluation suite addressing all three gaps. It comprises 300 human-verified tasks spanning 9 categories across three groups (general service orchestration, multimodal perception and generation, and multi-turn professional dialogue). Every agent action is recorded through three independent evidence channels (execution traces, audit logs, and environment snapshots), enabling trajectory-aware grading over 2,159 fine-grained rubric items. The scoring protocol evaluates Completion, Safety, and Robustness, reporting Average Score, Pass@k, and Pass^k across three trials to distinguish genuine capability from lucky outcomes. Experiments on 14 frontier models reveal that: (1) trajectory-opaque evaluation is systematically unreliable, missing 44% of safety violations and 13% of robustness failures that our hybrid pipeline catches; (2) controlled error injection primarily degrades consistency rather than peak capability, with Pass^3 dropping up to 24% while Pass@3 remains stable; (3) multimodal performance varies sharply, with most models performing poorer on video than on document or image, and no single model dominating across all modalities. Beyond benchmarking, Claw-Eval highlights actionable directions for agent development, shedding light on what it takes to build agents that are not only capable but reliably deployable.
